These raised, semi-translucent borders are a classic hallmark of this slow-growing malignancy. Everted edges (Option A) are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma, where the tissue is growing outward. Sloping edges (Option C) are typical of healing venous ulcers. Punched-out edges (Option D) are seen in trophic or syphilitic ulcers, which appear deep and cleanly cut. Recognizing these edge characteristics is fundamental for the clinical diagnosis of chronic skin lesions. A rodent ulcer, while locally invasive, rarely metastasizes but can cause significant tissue destruction if left untreated. It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Definitive management involves wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery to ensure clear margins while preserving healthy tissue

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following deficiencies causes follicular hyperkeratosis?
questions.explanation: Follicular hyperkeratosis (also known as phrynoderma or "toad skin") is a skin condition characterized by the excessive development of keratin in hair follicles. It is a classic dermatological manifestation of Vitamin A deficiency. Vitamin A is essential for the normal differentiation and maintenance of epithelial tissues; its lack leads to squamous metaplasia and keratin buildup. While Vitamin C deficiency (Option B, scurvy) causes "corkscrew hairs" and perifollicular hemorrhage, it does not cause primary follicular hyperkeratosis. Vitamin E (Option C) and Vitamin B6 (Option D) deficiencies do not have this specific cutaneous presentation. Follicular hyperkeratosis typically appears as small, firm, rough papules on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and the back. It is often accompanied by other signs of Vitamin A lack, such as night blindness or conjunctival xerosis. Treatment involves dietary improvements and oral Vitamin A supplementation, which usually results in a slow resolution of the skin changes

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The condition shown in the image below is seen in which vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates Casal’s necklace, which is the characteristic dermatological marker of Pellagra, caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3). Pellagra is famously identified by the "3 Ds" triad: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia. The dermatitis is photosensitive and well-demarcated, typically appearing around the neck (Casal's necklace) and on the dorsum of the hands and feet. Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6, Option A) and Riboflavin (Vitamin B2, Option D) deficiencies cause angular cheilitis and stomatitis but not this specific photosensitive rash. Cobalamin (Vitamin B12, Option B) deficiency results in megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms. Pellagra is most common in populations where maize (corn) is the primary staple, as maize is deficient in both niacin and its precursor amino acid, tryptophan. Treatment with oral nicotinamide provides rapid relief of systemic symptoms and gradual healing of the skin lesions. Recognizing this "necklace" pattern is essential for identifying nutritional deficiency in high-risk patients like chronic alcoholics

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most probable diagnosis of given image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a heliotrope rash—a characteristic violaceous/purple discoloration of the upper eyelids, often accompanied by periorbital edema. This rash is a pathognomonic skin finding for Dermatomyositis, an autoimmune inflammatory myopathy. Other classic skin features include Gottron papules over the knuckles and a "shawl sign" on the back. Polymyositis (Option A) involves similar muscle weakness but lacks the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis. Inclusion body myositis (Option C) typically affects older males and involves distal muscle weakness without a primary rash. Discoid lupus erythematosus (Option D) presents with well-defined, scarred plaques, usually in different facial locations than the eyelids. Dermatomyositis requires a comprehensive workup because it is associated with an increased risk of internal malignancies, particularly in older adults. Management involves high-dose corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents. The heliotrope rash is the key clinical anchor for differentiating these inflammatory muscle diseases

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not used in the treatment of acne vulgaris?
questions.explanation: Topical Fluocinolone is a potent corticosteroid. It is NOT used for the treatment of acne vulgaris; in fact, the prolonged use of topical steroids on the face can actually cause or worsen an acneiform eruption known as "steroid-induced acne". Benzoyl peroxide (Option A) is a standard antibacterial and comedolytic agent used for mild-to-moderate acne. Tazarotene (Option C) is a topical retinoid that is highly effective at normalizing follicular keratinization. Topical antibiotics (Option D, like clindamycin or erythromycin) are standard for reducing C. acnes colonization and inflammation. Effective acne management relies on targeting the four pathogenic factors: follicular hyperkeratosis, sebum production, bacterial colonization, and inflammation. Corticosteroids like fluocinolone should be avoided in acne patients unless being used briefly to manage a severe "flare" triggered by other treatments (e.g., acne fulminans). Therefore, fluocinolone is the correct "incorrect" drug for standard acne therapy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most probable diagnosis of given image?
questions.explanation: The image displays Milia, which are extremely common, benign neonatal skin findings. They appear as tiny (1–2 mm), pearly white or yellowish papules, most commonly seen on the nose, cheeks, and chin of newborns. They represent small epidermal inclusion cysts filled with keratin. Erythema toxicum neonatorum (Option A) appears as erythematous macules with central yellow papules or pustules, usually on the trunk. Pustular melanosis (Option B) involves fragile pustules that rupture to leave hyperpigmented macules. Mongolian spots (Option C) are bluish-grey patches of congenital dermal melanocytosis, typically found on the sacral area. Milia are completely asymptomatic and require no treatment, as they typically resolve spontaneously within the first few weeks of life as the skin pores open and mature. Recognizing these benign "normal" newborn rashes is essential for pediatricians and midwives to provide appropriate reassurance to anxious parents

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During epidural anesthesia, which of the following layers is least likely to be punctured?
questions.explanation: In epidural anesthesia, the goal is to place the local anesthetic into the potential space just outside the dural sac. Therefore, the Arachnoid mater is the layer least likely to be punctured; if the arachnoid is breached, the procedure becomes a spinal (subarachnoid) block rather than an epidural. During a standard midline approach, the needle passes through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, Supraspinatus ligament (Option C), interspinatus ligament, and finally the Ligamentum flavum (Option B) to reach the epidural space. The Infraspinatus (Option D) is a muscle of the rotator cuff in the shoulder and is entirely irrelevant to spinal or epidural anatomy. Successful epidural placement relies on the "loss of resistance" technique as the needle exits the dense ligamentum flavum. Accidental puncture of the dura/arachnoid is a recognized complication known as a "dural tap," which can lead to a significant post-dural puncture headache. Knowledge of these spinal layers is critical for safe regional anesthesia

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which inhalational anesthetic agent has a blood–gas partition coefficient most similar to that of nitrous oxide?
questions.explanation: The blood-gas partition coefficient determines the solubility of an anesthetic in the blood and directly influences the speed of induction and emergence. Nitrous oxide has a very low coefficient (approximately 0.47), which explains its rapid effects. Among the volatile agents, Desflurane has the most similar coefficient (approximately 0.42), making it the least soluble volatile agent. Sevoflurane (Option C) has a slightly higher coefficient of 0.65. Isoflurane (Option A) has a coefficient of 1.4, and Halothane (Option D) is the most soluble with a coefficient of 2.4, leading to a much slower recovery. Because desflurane is so insoluble, it provides the fastest emergence of all currently used volatile agents, allowing patients to wake up very quickly even after long procedures. However, its use is limited by its high cost and pungent odor, which can cause airway irritation. Identifying these coefficients is essential for understanding the clinical pharmacokinetics of inhalation anesthesia

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is considered a contraindication to the use of bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP)?
questions.explanation: Bi-level Positive Airway Pressure (BiPAP) is a form of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) that requires the patient to be alert, cooperative, and able to protect their own airway. Therefore, being unconscious or heavily sedated is an absolute contraindication for its use. In such patients, BiPAP carries a high risk of aspiration and gastric insufflation; they require invasive endotracheal intubation instead. Obstructive sleep apnea (Option A) is a primary indication for positive pressure therapy (usually CPAP or BiPAP). Low oxygen levels (hypoxia) (Option D) are often the very reason BiPAP is initiated (e.g., in COPD or heart failure). High oxygen levels (Option C) are not a direct contraindication, although therapy would be unnecessary if oxygenation is normal. Other contraindications for BiPAP include severe facial trauma, vomiting, or excessive secretions. The success of BiPAP depends heavily on the patient's ability to synchronize with the machine and maintain their airway reflexes. Clinicians must meticulously screen patients before initiating non-invasive support

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the hemorrhage shown in the following image?
questions.explanation: Subdural hemorrhage The CT image shows a crescent-shaped (concave) hyperdense collection along the surface of the brain, which is characteristic of a subdural hemorrhage (SDH). This occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, commonly following trauma. The blood spreads over the cerebral convexity and is not limited by suture lines, but it is restricted by dural reflections like the falx cerebri. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Extradural (epidural) hemorrhage: Appears biconvex (lens-shaped) and is limited by sutures; usually due to middle meningeal artery injury. (B) Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Blood is seen in sulci and basal cisterns (star-shaped pattern), not as a crescentic collection. (C) Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Appears as a localized hyperdense lesion within brain tissue, not along the surface.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radioisotope used in PET-CT scan?
questions.explanation: The most common and standard radioisotope used in PET-CT scanning for oncological and metabolic imaging is Fluorine-18, typically attached to a glucose analog known as 18F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose). As established in Q.281, cancer cells uptake this glucose analog at high rates, which the PET scanner detects as "hot spots." Iodine (Option B, typically I-131) is used primarily for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid conditions. Radium (Option C) and Cesium-131 (Option D) are used in brachytherapy for cancer treatment, not as diagnostic tracers for PET imaging. 18F-FDG has a half-life of approximately 110 minutes, allowing enough time for production, transport, and imaging while ensuring a relatively low radiation dose to the patient. PET-CT is an essential tool for staging malignancies, monitoring therapy response, and identifying hidden metastases. Clinicians must consider physiological uptake in the brain and heart when interpreting FDG-PET results

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions exhibit the given radiological findings?
questions.explanation: The Chest X-ray demonstrates multiple, large, discrete, and well-circumscribed bilateral nodules, a classic finding known as "cannon-ball metastasis". This pattern is highly characteristic of Lung metastasis, most commonly originating from primary tumors such as renal cell carcinoma, testicular seminoma, or choriocarcinoma. Miliary TB (Option A) presents with numerous tiny (1–2 mm), millet-seed-like nodules distributed evenly throughout the lungs. Aspergillosis (Option B) usually presents as a mass within a pre-existing cavity or as areas of consolidation. Consolidation (Option C) appears as a more confluent, ill-defined area of opacity, often within a single lobe, rather than multiple discrete round masses. Cannon-ball metastases typically signify an advanced, disseminated malignancy. Identifying this specific radiological pattern is a high-yield clinical clue that directs the search for a primary malignancy elsewhere in the body

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the least radiosensitive cell?
questions.explanation: Radiosensitivity depends on the rate of cell division and level of differentiation (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau). Cells that divide rapidly are more radiosensitive, while non-dividing, mature cells are more radioresistant. Platelets are considered the least radiosensitive because they are non-dividing cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes and have minimal metabolic and genetic activity. Since they do not undergo mitosis, they are less affected by radiation compared to other blood cells. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Red blood cells: Although anucleate and resistant, they are not considered the least radiosensitive in standard exam context. (C) Lymphocytes: Among the most radiosensitive cells due to high turnover and metabolic activity. (D) Neutrophils: Derived from actively dividing precursors, making them more radiosensitive than platelets

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the ideal thickness of lead aprons for personnel working in a radiology department?
questions.explanation: In the field of radiation protection, the goal is to reduce occupational exposure as much as possible (ALARA principle). For the majority of diagnostic radiology workers, a lead apron with a thickness of 0.5 mm lead equivalent is considered the ideal standard. This thickness provides an excellent balance between radiation attenuation and the physical comfort of the wearer; a 0.5 mm apron can block approximately 95–99% of the scattered X-ray radiation encountered in typical diagnostic settings. While a 1 mm apron (Option B) would provide even higher protection, it is significantly heavier and can cause orthopedic issues with prolonged use. 0.75 mm (Option C) and 2 mm (Option D) are not standard requirements for general diagnostic work. Proper storage (hanging rather than folding) is also essential to prevent the lead from cracking. Consistent use of these personal protective devices, along with thyroid shields and lead glasses, is mandatory for ensuring the long-term safety of radiology personnel

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following image shows which X-ray view?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the orientation of the skull for a Towne view (AP axial projection). In this view, the X-ray beam is angled caudally (downward), typically about 30° to the orbitomeatal line (OML), as shown by the green arrow passing from the frontal region toward the occipital bone. This projection is primarily used to visualize the occipital bone, foramen magnum, and posterior cranial fossa, and is especially helpful in assessing occipital fractures and posterior skull structures. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Waters view: Used for maxillary sinuses, with the head extended so the chin touches the cassette (occipitomental view). (B) Caldwell view: An AP projection with slight caudal angulation (15°), mainly for frontal sinuses and orbits. (D) Hirtz view (submentovertex): Beam passes from below the chin upward, used to visualize the base of the skull

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The chest X-ray below shows a right-sided lung white-out with contralateral tracheal deviation. In which condition is this finding typically seen?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows right-sided white-out (complete opacification) with contralateral (leftward) tracheal deviation. This indicates a space-occupying lesion causing a mass effect, which pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. White-out lung + trachea shifted away (contralateral) → suggests increased volume/pressure on that side This is typical of large pleural effusion or thoracic mass Why other options are incorrect: (A) Pneumothorax:Would show a hyperlucent (black) hemithorax, not white-out. (B) Consolidation:Causes white-out but usually no significant tracheal shift. (C) Collapse (atelectasis):Leads to tracheal deviation toward the same side (volume loss), not away. Therefore, contralateral deviation with white-out strongly points to a thoracic mass effect (most appropriate option here)

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fatigue and shortness of breath. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are noted. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical features—fatigue, dyspnea, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds—suggest impaired cardiac filling. The X-ray described is consistent with constrictive pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes thickened and non-compliant, restricting ventricular filling. A key radiological feature is the “egg in cup” appearance, where the heart appears relatively normal or mildly enlarged but is surrounded by a rigid pericardium. Unlike pericardial effusion, there is no globular (water bottle) enlargement. The pathology involves fibrosis and sometimes calcification of the pericardium, leading to diastolic dysfunction. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Acute pericarditis: Typically shows a flask-shaped enlarged cardiac silhouette due to pericardial effusion, which is not seen here. (B) Bronchial asthma: Shows hyperinflated lungs, not cardiac changes. (D) Atrial myxoma: May cause intracardiac obstruction but does not produce this characteristic X-ray appearance

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the arrow-marked chamber?
questions.explanation: This is an axial CT scan of the thorax. On axial imaging, anatomical orientation is such that the anterior structures are at the top of the image, and the right side of the patient appears on the left side of the image. The arrow points to a chamber located anteriorly and somewhat toward the patient’s right side, which corresponds to the right ventricle (RV). The right ventricle forms the most anterior part of the heart and lies just behind the sternum, making it the chamber most commonly seen in the anterior position on CT. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Right atrium: Located more right-sided and slightly posterior, not the most anterior chamber. (B) Left atrium: Lies posteriorly, forming the base of the heart. (D) Left ventricle: Located more posterior and left-sided, forming the apex but not the most anterior structure. Thus, the arrow-marked chamber is the right ventricle

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which type of intracranial hemorrhage is most likely shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: A subdural hematoma occurs due to tearing of bridging veins, leading to accumulation of venous blood between the dura mater and arachnoid mater. On NCCT, it appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity that can cross suture lines, a key distinguishing feature. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Extradural hemorrhage: Shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense lesion and does not cross suture lines. (B) Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Appears as diffuse hyperdensity in sulci and basal cisterns, not a localized crescent-shaped collection. (D) Intraparenchymal hemorrhage: Seen as a hyperdense lesion within brain tissue, often with surrounding edema. Thus, based on standard imaging features, the correct diagnosis is subdural hematoma

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A barium swallow study of a woman with dysphagia is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The barium swallow image shows the pathognomonic "bird’s beak sign"—a massive dilation of the proximal esophagus ending in a smooth, symmetric, tapering narrowing at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). This is the classic radiological finding for Achalasia, a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the failure of the LES to relax and the absence of peristalsis. Distal esophageal spasm (Option B) typically shows a "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow. Jackhammer esophagus (Option C) is a hypercontractile disorder that may show high-pressure segments but not the specific bird's beak narrowing. Clinically, achalasia presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset, often accompanied by regurgitation and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed by esophageal manometry, which is the gold standard. Management includes pneumatic dilation, botulinum toxin injection, or definitive surgical Heller’s myotomy. The bird's beak sign is one of the most reliable and high-yield radiological identifiers in gastroenterology

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify pancreas, liver, and spleen?
questions.explanation: On a standard axial CT scan of the upper abdomen, the organs are identified by their characteristic positions: 1. A (Liver): The largest solid organ, occupying the right upper quadrant. 2. B (Pancreas): A lobulated, retroperitoneal organ that lies transversely across the midline, posterior to the stomach. 3. C (Spleen): A smaller, solid organ located in the left upper quadrant, lateral to the tail of the pancreas. Options B, C, and D provide incorrect assignments for these anatomical landmarks. Accurately identifying these organs is the first step in abdominal CT interpretation. The liver is typically on the left side of the image (the patient's right). The pancreas is often identified by its proximity to the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric artery. The spleen's location in the far left is a reliable marker. This anatomical spatial reasoning is a fundamental skill for medical board exams and clinical radiology practice

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds are noted. A chest X-ray is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with shortness of breath, fatigue, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds, which strongly suggest chronic cardiac compression. These findings are classical for constrictive pericarditis, where the pericardium becomes thickened, fibrotic, and sometimes calcified, restricting normal cardiac filling. The chest X-ray in such cases often shows pericardial calcification, which appears as curvilinear radio-opaque shadows around the cardiac silhouette. This radiological feature is highly suggestive of constrictive pericarditis and helps differentiate it from other causes of heart failure. Why other options are wrong: (B) Bronchial asthma : Presents with wheezing and hyperinflated lungs, not JVD or muffled heart sounds (C) Acute pericarditis : Causes chest pain and pericardial effusion but not calcification (D) Atrial myxoma : May cause obstruction but does not show pericardial calcification on X-ray

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radioactive isotope used for teletherapy?
questions.explanation: Teletherapy refers to external beam radiation therapy where the radiation source is located at a distance from the patient. Cobalt-60 is the standard radioactive isotope used for teletherapy in many centers (specifically in Cobalt units). It emits high-energy gamma rays and has a half-life of 5.27 years. Iridium-192 (Option A) and Iodine-125 (Option B) are characteristically used for brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumor. Iodine-131 (Option D) is an unsealed isotope used for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid diseases, not for external teletherapy. While linear accelerators (LINACs) have largely replaced cobalt units in high-resource settings, Cobalt-60 remains a vital isotope for teletherapy globally due to its reliability and simpler maintenance. Understanding the differences between teletherapy and brachytherapy isotopes is a core concept in clinical oncology and radiotherapy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which condition is characterized by the presence of an empty delta sign on imaging?
questions.explanation: The "empty delta sign" is the pathognomonic radiological finding for Cerebral Venous (Sinus) Thrombosis on a contrast-enhanced CT scan. It refers to a triangular area of non-enhancement (the thrombus) surrounded by the enhancing wall of the superior sagittal sinus. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option A) presents with blood in the sulci and cisterns. Subdural hemorrhage (Option B) is a crescentic blood collection, and Intra parenchymal hemorrhage (Option D) is blood within the brain tissue. Cerebral venous thrombosis is a common cause of stroke in young adults, particularly women (associated with pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or dehydration). Patients typically present with headache, seizures, and focal deficits. While the empty delta sign is specific, the gold standard for diagnosis is MR venography (MRV). Prompt treatment with anticoagulation (even in the presence of venous hemorrhage) is essential to prevent venous infarction and improve neurological outcomes

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient reports the belief that his thoughts and feelings are being controlled or influenced by an external agency. What is this psychopathological phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: The belief that one's feelings, thoughts, or movements are being controlled or influenced by an external agency is known as a Passivity phenomenon (or delusion of control). This is one of Schneider’s First-Rank Symptoms of schizophrenia. Delusion of nihilism (Option A, Cotard’s syndrome) involves the belief that one is dead or that the world doesn't exist. Delusion of reference (Option B) is the belief that neutral events (like news broadcasts) have a special, personal meaning meant only for the patient. Othello syndrome (Option C) is a delusion of morbid jealousy, where the patient is convinced of a partner's infidelity without cause. Passivity phenomena are highly diagnostic for psychotic disorders. The patient may feel like a "puppet," with their will being overridden by outside forces. Identifying these core psychotic features is essential for differentiating schizophrenia from other mental health conditions and starting appropriate antipsychotic management

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Atypical antipsychotic with least metabolic side effects?
questions.explanation: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are generally associated with metabolic side effects like weight gain and diabetes. Among the options, Ziprasidone is known for having the least metabolic side effects, being largely weight-neutral. Haloperidol (Option A) is a first-generation antipsychotic; while it has low metabolic risk, it has very high risks of extrapyramidal side effects. Risperidone (Option B) and Quetiapine (Option D) have moderate-to-high risks of metabolic syndrome and weight gain. Clozapine and Olanzapine (not listed) have the highest risk. While ziprasidone is metabolic-safe, it carries a unique risk of dose-dependent QT interval prolongation, requiring cardiac monitoring in high-risk patients. For a patient already suffering from obesity or diabetes, choosing a "metabolic-friendly" drug like ziprasidone or aripiprazole is a critical part of holistic psychiatric management to ensure physical health along with mental stability

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents to the hospital claiming to be experiencing a cardiac arrest. After a thorough medical evaluation, he is found to be physically healthy but refuses to leave the hospital. He reports a recent history of being held at gunpoint during a robbery. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with acute psychological distress following a life-threatening traumatic event (being held at gunpoint). His irrational belief of having a "cardiac arrest" and refusal to leave the hospital are manifestations of the intense anxiety and hyperarousal seen in Acute Stress Disorder (ASD). ASD is diagnosed when symptoms occur within one month of the trauma. If symptoms persist beyond one month, the diagnosis changes to Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Schizophrenia (Option B) is characterized by chronic hallucinations and delusions unrelated to a specific acute trauma. Avoidant personality disorder (Option C) is a long-term pattern of social inhibition. Delirium (Option D) involves an acute, fluctuating change in consciousness due to a medical cause. Management of ASD involves psychological first aid, trauma-focused therapy, and occasionally short-term benzodiazepines. The acute, trauma-linked nature of the symptoms is the key to this diagnosis

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient receiving the antipsychotic haloperidol develops acute dystonia. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle contractions, such as torticollis or oculogyric crisis) is a common and distressing extrapyramidal side effect of high-potency first-generation antipsychotics like Haloperidol. The next best step and standard acute treatment is the administration of an anticholinergic agent, such as Benztropine or Procyclidine, which rapidly reverses the muscle spasm. Fluphenazine (Option C) is another high-potency antipsychotic that would likely worsen the dystonia. Increasing the dose of haloperidol (Option D) is strictly contraindicated and would exacerbate the condition. Changing to clozapine (Option B) is a long-term strategy for refractory patients but is not the immediate treatment for an acute dystonic episode. After reversing the dystonia, the overall treatment plan should be reviewed, often by switching the patient to an atypical antipsychotic with lower extrapyramidal risk. Bedside recognition and rapid pharmacological reversal are essential for patient comfort and safety

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents to the psychiatric outpatient department with inattention at school, hyperactivity (excessive talking and difficulty remaining seated), aggressive behavior toward peers, and poor academic performance. Which drug is indicated for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: The child's symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity (hitting friends, excess talking), and impulsivity (cannot sit still) causing functional impairment in school are classic for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). The first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD in children aged 6 years and older is Methylphenidate, a CNS stimulant. It works by increasing the levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex, helping to improve focus and impulse control. Modafinil (Option B) is used for narcolepsy. Atenolol (Option C) is a beta-blocker. Amitriptyline (Option D) is a tricyclic antidepressant; while sometimes used off-label for ADHD, it is never the first-line choice. Management of ADHD also requires behavioral interventions and parent training. Long-term use of stimulants requires monitoring for side effects like suppressed appetite and growth. Methylphenidate remains the gold-standard treatment for pediatric ADHD

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia, currently on antipsychotic medication, develops acute dystonia. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: Acute dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotic therapy. The appropriate management involves using an anticholinergic medication. Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) is a standard anticholinergic drug used to treat and prevent dystonia and parkinsonian symptoms induced by antipsychotics. Fluphenazine (Option B) would likely worsen the EPS. Increasing the dose of haloperidol (Option C) is incorrect as it would increase the dopamine blockade responsible for the dystonia. Clozapine (Option D) is an atypical antipsychotic used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but is not the acute management for a dystonic crisis. Patients often receive these anticholinergics alongside their antipsychotic to maintain neurological stability. Clinicians must balance the benefits of symptom control with the anticholinergic side effects like dry mouth and blurred vision. Benzhexol remains a foundational tool in the management of antipsychotic side effects. **************
